title: Social feed with keyset pagination
scenario: Page 2,000 of the feed takes 4 seconds and new posts push duplicates onto the next page.
stack: Spring Boot 4.1.1 · Java 25 · JdbcClient · keyset (seek) pagination · row-value comparison · opaque cursors · PostgreSQL 17 · Testcontainers
simulation: Authors and posts are generated demo data (100,000 posts), not Chaupal's. There is no login; the feed is one public feed.

tabs.html:
Belongs in this tab

  • What we are building, and an everyday analogy

Level 1, about 5 minutes. Plain language: no code.

The problem in real life

  1. Scrolling the feed

    A Chaupal user scrolls for a long time. Each new page is "skip N posts, show 20".

  2. Slower and repeating

    Page 2,000 has to read and discard 40,000 posts first: four seconds. And when friends post while the user reads page 1, every post moves down: the bottom of page 1 shows up again at the top of page 2.

  3. The fix

    Each page says where it stopped: the last post's time and id. The next page asks for posts older than that one, which the index finds directly, whatever was posted in between.

Page by position in the data, not by counting rows.

What are we building?

GET /feed returns the newest posts and a nextCursor; GET /feed?cursor=… continues from there, at the same speed on page 2 and page 2,000.

An everyday analogy

Reading a long newspaper archive. Offset paging is "start from the first issue and count 40,000 pages". Keyset paging is a bookmark: "the issue after 1 October, 05:33", and you open it there.

How it works in 4 steps

  1. First page: the newest posts, one more than asked.
  2. If there is that extra post, there is a next page: the cursor is the last shown post's time and id.
  3. Next page: posts older than the cursor's post, in the same order, straight from the index.
  4. The end: fewer posts than asked, and no cursor.
Check yourself: why does the cursor need the id, and not just the time?

Five posts can share one second. If page 1 ends at the second of those five, "older than this time" skips the other four. "Older than (this time, this id)" continues with them. The test shows the four lost posts.

What this station is not

  • No personal feed. One public feed; following people is a filter (Practice 1).
  • No ranking. Newest first only.
  • No page numbers. Keyset paging cannot jump to page 517, by design.

Key terms

TermSimple meaningEveryday exampleIn this project
Offset paging"Skip the first N, give me the next 20."Counting 40,000 envelopes to reach the 40,001st.the old feed: OFFSET
Keyset (seek) paging"Give me the 20 that come after this one."A bookmark: open the book where you stopped.WHERE (created_at, id) < (…)
CursorA token saying where the last page stopped.The bookmark itself.nextCursor
OpaqueClients pass it back unchanged and do not read it.A cloakroom token: you hand it back, you do not decode it.base64url of v1:1790832799000000:99998
Tie-breakingA second key for rows with the same first key.Two posts in the same second, told apart by id.id after created_at
Row-value comparisonComparing several columns at once, in order.Compare dates; if equal, compare numbers.(created_at, id) < (:t, :id)

tabs.html:
Belongs in this tab

  • 1. Business problem
  • 2. Acceptance criteria
  • 3. Requirements
  • 4. Learning objectives

Level 2. What a teammate hands you before you build.

Business problem

Chaupal (a fictional social app) pages its feed with OFFSET. Page 2,000 takes 4 seconds, and new posts push duplicates onto the next page.

Acceptance criteria

Demo data: 100,000 posts, five per second, from 1 October 2026 00:00 UTC.

  1. Given no cursor, then posts 100000 down to 99981 and a nextCursor.
  2. Given that cursor, then the next posts with no gap and no repeat, even if posts were added meanwhile.
  3. Given a page boundary inside one second, then the posts sharing that second still appear.
  4. Given the last page, then nextCursor is null; a cursor past the oldest post gives an empty page.
  5. Given a cursor this feed did not make, or a limit outside 1 to 50, then 400.
  6. Given page 2,000, then the database reads about one page of rows, not 40,000.

Requirements

  • Order by (created_at, id), both descending, everywhere.
  • The cursor holds both values; it is opaque and versioned.
  • No count query: one extra row tells whether more follow.
  • An index matches the order.

Learning objectives

  • Measure what OFFSET costs.
  • Write a keyset page with a row-value comparison.
  • Design an opaque cursor with a tie-breaker.
  • Know what keyset paging cannot do.

The trap

Plausible but wrong

Deep OFFSET paging that gets slower page by page and duplicates new posts.

  • Slower. OFFSET 40000 means reading 40,000 rows in order and throwing them away. In the captured plans, the scans produced 40,020 rows for the offset page and 21 for the keyset page (including the one-row lookup of the cursor's post).
  • Repeats. Three new posts move everything down by three. Page 2 by offset starts with the last three posts of page 1; the keyset page starts after the last post the reader saw.
  • The first cursor people write. "Older than this time" skips the posts that share the last post's second. Here, four of them.

While building, each fix was undone once: dropping the id from the cursor turned 4 tests red; not fetching the extra row 5; accepting any decoded text as a cursor 1; dropping the index 1.

package com.chaupal.feed;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.AfterEach;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import tools.jackson.databind.JsonNode;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.OffsetDateTime;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

/** Written first. The old OFFSET feed and a time-only cursor, against the keyset feed, on the same 100,000 posts. */
class OffsetPagingTrapTest extends ApiTest {

    static final String OFFSET_PAGE = Feed.FIRST.replace("LIMIT :n", "LIMIT :n OFFSET :skip");

    @AfterEach
    void removeNewPosts() {
        jdbc.sql("DELETE FROM posts WHERE body LIKE 'Test new post%'").update();
    }

    private List<Long> offsetPage(int page, int size) {
        return jdbc.sql(OFFSET_PAGE).param("n", size).param("skip", page * size).query((rs, i) -> rs.getLong("id")).list();
    }

    private static List<Long> ids(JsonNode page) {
        List<Long> ids = new ArrayList<>();
        page.get("posts").forEach(p -> ids.add(p.get("id").asLong()));
        return ids;
    }

    @Test
    void page2000ByOffsetReadsEveryPostBeforeIt() {
        // Page 2,000 of 20: the old feed reads and throws away 40,000 posts (and their authors) to return 20.
        long offset = rowsRead(OFFSET_PAGE, Map.of("n", 20, "skip", 40_000));
        // The same page by keyset: start after post 60,001, the last one on page 1,999.
        Instant at = jdbc.sql("SELECT created_at FROM posts WHERE id = 60001").query(OffsetDateTime.class).single().toInstant();
        long keyset = rowsRead(Feed.AFTER, Map.of("n", 21, "createdAt", OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(at, ZoneOffset.UTC), "id", 60001L));
        assertThat(offset).isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(40_020);
        assertThat(keyset).isLessThanOrEqualTo(100);
    }

    @Test
    void newPostsPushRepeatsOntoTheNextOffsetPage() throws Exception {
        List<Long> page1 = offsetPage(0, 20);
        JsonNode keysetPage1 = getFeed(null, 20);
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
            post("Test new post " + i);   // three people post while the reader looks at page 1
        }
        List<Long> page2 = offsetPage(1, 20);
        assertThat(page2.subList(0, 3)).isEqualTo(page1.subList(17, 20));   // the last three of page 1, again

        List<Long> keysetPage2 = ids(getFeed(keysetPage1.get("nextCursor").asString(), 20));
        assertThat(keysetPage2).doesNotContainAnyElementsOf(ids(keysetPage1));
        assertThat(keysetPage2.getFirst()).isEqualTo(99980);   // straight on from 99981, new posts or not
    }

    @Test
    void aCursorWithTheTimeAloneSkipsPostsFromTheSameSecond() throws Exception {
        JsonNode first = getFeed(null, 7);   // ends at post 99994; posts 99990 to 99993 share its second
        Instant last = Instant.parse(first.get("posts").get(6).get("createdAt").asString());
        List<Long> timeOnly = jdbc.sql(Feed.FIRST.replace("ORDER BY", "WHERE p.created_at < :createdAt ORDER BY"))
                .param("createdAt", OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(last, ZoneOffset.UTC)).param("n", 7).query((rs, i) -> rs.getLong("id")).list();
        assertThat(timeOnly.getFirst()).isEqualTo(99989);   // 99990 to 99993 never shown
        assertThat(ids(getFeed(first.get("nextCursor").asString(), 7))).startsWith(99993L, 99992L, 99991L, 99990L, 99989L);
    }
}

Does
Checks the limit and decodes the cursor.
Why
A bad cursor is a 400 before any query.
Without it
A garbage cursor reaching SQL.
package com.chaupal.feed;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.Max;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Min;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Size;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
class FeedController {

    private final Feed feed;

    FeedController(Feed feed) {
        this.feed = feed;
    }

    /** Newest first. Pass the response's nextCursor to get the following page; null means the end. */
    @GetMapping("/feed")
    Feed.Page feed(@RequestParam(required = false) @Size(max = 100) String cursor,
                   @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") @Min(1) @Max(50) int limit) {
        return feed.page(cursor == null ? null : Cursor.decode(cursor), limit);
    }
}

src/main/java/com/chaupal/feed/Cursor.java

Does
Encodes and decodes the position: version, time in microseconds, id.
Why
Opaque and versioned; parsed strictly.
Without it
Clients building offsets or timestamps themselves.
  • Microseconds, because PostgreSQL stores timestamptz to the microsecond: a millisecond cursor would round and skip or repeat posts.
  • Not signed: a client can decode it, and can only ask for a position it could reach by scrolling.
package com.chaupal.feed;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.web.server.ResponseStatusException;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;
import java.util.Base64;
import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

/**
 * Where the last page stopped: the last post's time and id. Opaque to clients (base64url of "v1:micros:id"), so they
 * pass it back unchanged and the server can change its contents later. Not a secret: anyone can decode it.
 */
record Cursor(Instant createdAt, long id) {

    private static final Pattern FORMAT = Pattern.compile("v1:(-?\\d{1,18}):(\\d{1,18})");

    String encode() {
        long micros = ChronoUnit.MICROS.between(Instant.EPOCH, createdAt);
        return Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(("v1:" + micros + ":" + id).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII));
    }

    static Cursor decode(String text) {
        try {
            Matcher m = FORMAT.matcher(new String(Base64.getUrlDecoder().decode(text), StandardCharsets.US_ASCII));
            if (m.matches()) {
                return new Cursor(Instant.EPOCH.plus(Long.parseLong(m.group(1)), ChronoUnit.MICROS), Long.parseLong(m.group(2)));
            }
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            // not base64: answered below like any other bad cursor
        }
        throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Not a cursor from this feed; start again without one");
    }
}

src/main/java/com/chaupal/feed/Feed.java

Does
The first page and the seek, one row more than asked.
Why
The row-value comparison matches the index's order, so the page starts where the cursor points.
Without it
OFFSET, and a count query to know about the next page.
package com.chaupal.feed;

import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.OffsetDateTime;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;
import java.util.List;

@Service
class Feed {

    record Post(long id, String author, String body, Instant createdAt) {
    }

    record Page(List<Post> posts, String nextCursor) {
    }

    static final String FIRST = """
            SELECT p.id, a.handle AS author, p.body, p.created_at FROM posts p JOIN authors a ON a.id = p.author_id
            ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC LIMIT :n""";

    /** Seek: start right after the cursor's post, in the index's order. No OFFSET, so no rows are read and thrown away. */
    static final String AFTER = """
            SELECT p.id, a.handle AS author, p.body, p.created_at FROM posts p JOIN authors a ON a.id = p.author_id
            WHERE (p.created_at, p.id) < (:createdAt, :id)
            ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC LIMIT :n""";

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;

    Feed(JdbcClient jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    Page page(Cursor after, int limit) {
        // One row more than asked: if it exists, there is a next page, and no count is needed.
        List<Post> rows = (after == null ? jdbc.sql(FIRST)
                : jdbc.sql(AFTER).param("createdAt", OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(after.createdAt(), ZoneOffset.UTC)).param("id", after.id()))
                .param("n", limit + 1).query(Post.class).list();
        if (rows.size() <= limit) {
            return new Page(rows, null);
        }
        List<Post> page = rows.subList(0, limit);
        Post last = page.getLast();
        return new Page(page, new Cursor(last.createdAt(), last.id()).encode());
    }
}

src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__posts.sql

Does
Tables, named constraints and the feed index.
Why
posts_feed (created_at, id) read backwards is the feed.
Without it
A sort of every post for every page.
CREATE TABLE authors (
    id     BIGINT      PRIMARY KEY,
    handle VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL CONSTRAINT authors_handle_unique UNIQUE
                               CONSTRAINT authors_handle_shape CHECK (handle ~ '^[a-z0-9_]{3,30}$')
);

CREATE TABLE posts (
    id         BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    author_id  BIGINT        NOT NULL CONSTRAINT posts_author_fk REFERENCES authors (id),
    body       VARCHAR(500)  NOT NULL CONSTRAINT posts_body_not_blank CHECK (btrim(body) <> ''),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ   NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- The feed's order, newest first: read backwards, (created_at, id) finds "the posts after this one" directly.
CREATE INDEX posts_feed ON posts (created_at, id);

src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__demo_posts.sql

4 authors and 100,000 posts, five per second.

INSERT INTO authors (id, handle) VALUES (1, 'asha_writes'), (2, 'kabir'), (3, 'meera_k'), (4, 'ravi_07');

-- 100,000 posts over about 5.5 hours, five per second: posts made in the same second share a timestamp,
-- as they do when an app imports a batch or a server's clock only has second precision.
INSERT INTO posts (author_id, body, created_at)
SELECT g % 4 + 1, 'Post number ' || g, TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-10-01 00:00:00+00' + make_interval(secs => g / 5)
FROM generate_series(1, 100000) AS g;
ANALYZE posts;

    static final String OFFSET_PAGE = Feed.FIRST.replace("LIMIT :n", "LIMIT :n OFFSET :skip");

    @AfterEach
    void removeNewPosts() {
        jdbc.sql("DELETE FROM posts WHERE body LIKE 'Test new post%'").update();
    }

    private List<Long> offsetPage(int page, int size) {
        return jdbc.sql(OFFSET_PAGE).param("n", size).param("skip", page * size).query((rs, i) -> rs.getLong("id")).list();
    }

    private static List<Long> ids(JsonNode page) {
        List<Long> ids = new ArrayList<>();
        page.get("posts").forEach(p -> ids.add(p.get("id").asLong()));
        return ids;
    }

    @Test
    void page2000ByOffsetReadsEveryPostBeforeIt() {
        // Page 2,000 of 20: the old feed reads and throws away 40,000 posts (and their authors) to return 20.
        long offset = rowsRead(OFFSET_PAGE, Map.of("n", 20, "skip", 40_000));
        // The same page by keyset: start after post 60,001, the last one on page 1,999.
        Instant at = jdbc.sql("SELECT created_at FROM posts WHERE id = 60001").query(OffsetDateTime.class).single().toInstant();
        long keyset = rowsRead(Feed.AFTER, Map.of("n", 21, "createdAt", OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(at, ZoneOffset.UTC), "id", 60001L));
        assertThat(offset).isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(40_020);
        assertThat(keyset).isLessThanOrEqualTo(100);
    }

    @Test
    void newPostsPushRepeatsOntoTheNextOffsetPage() throws Exception {
        List<Long> page1 = offsetPage(0, 20);
        JsonNode keysetPage1 = getFeed(null, 20);
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
            post("Test new post " + i);   // three people post while the reader looks at page 1
        }
        List<Long> page2 = offsetPage(1, 20);
        assertThat(page2.subList(0, 3)).isEqualTo(page1.subList(17, 20));   // the last three of page 1, again

        List<Long> keysetPage2 = ids(getFeed(keysetPage1.get("nextCursor").asString(), 20));
        assertThat(keysetPage2).doesNotContainAnyElementsOf(ids(keysetPage1));
        assertThat(keysetPage2.getFirst()).isEqualTo(99980);   // straight on from 99981, new posts or not
    }

    @Test
    void aCursorWithTheTimeAloneSkipsPostsFromTheSameSecond() throws Exception {
        JsonNode first = getFeed(null, 7);   // ends at post 99994; posts 99990 to 99993 share its second
        Instant last = Instant.parse(first.get("posts").get(6).get("createdAt").asString());
        List<Long> timeOnly = jdbc.sql(Feed.FIRST.replace("ORDER BY", "WHERE p.created_at < :createdAt ORDER BY"))
                .param("createdAt", OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(last, ZoneOffset.UTC)).param("n", 7).query((rs, i) -> rs.getLong("id")).list();
        assertThat(timeOnly.getFirst()).isEqualTo(99989);   // 99990 to 99993 never shown
        assertThat(ids(getFeed(first.get("nextCursor").asString(), 7))).startsWith(99993L, 99992L, 99991L, 99990L, 99989L);
    }
}

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

/** The rules as PostgreSQL enforces them, with plain SQL; test rows start with "Test" and are removed afterwards. */
class PostDatabaseTest extends ApiTest {

    @AfterEach
    void removeTestRows() {
        jdbc.sql("DELETE FROM posts WHERE body LIKE 'Test%'").update();
        jdbc.sql("DELETE FROM authors WHERE id >= 100").update();
    }

    @Test
    void namedConstraintsHoldWithoutJava() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO posts (author_id, body) VALUES (1, '   ')").update())
                .isInstanceOf(DataAccessException.class).hasMessageContaining("posts_body_not_blank");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO posts (author_id, body) VALUES (99, 'Test orphan')").update()).hasMessageContaining("posts_author_fk");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO authors (id, handle) VALUES (100, 'Asha Writes')").update()).hasMessageContaining("authors_handle_shape");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO authors (id, handle) VALUES (100, 'kabir')").update()).hasMessageContaining("authors_handle_unique");
    }

    @Test
    void aNewPostIsStampedByTheDatabaseAndTopsTheFeed() throws Exception {
        jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO posts (author_id, body) VALUES (2, 'Test hello Chaupal')").update();   // created_at = now(), after every demo post
        assertThat(getFeed(null, 1).get("posts").get(0).get("body").asString()).isEqualTo("Test hello Chaupal");
    }

    @Test
    void aNewAuthorWithAnOrphanPostIsNotAddedAtAll() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> transaction.executeWithoutResult(tx -> {
            jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO authors (id, handle) VALUES (100, 'test_author')").update();
            jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO posts (author_id, body) VALUES (100, 'Test first post')").update();
            jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO posts (author_id, body) VALUES (101, 'Test wrong author')").update();
        })).hasMessageContaining("posts_author_fk");
        assertThat(jdbc.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM authors WHERE id = 100").query(Long.class).single()).isZero();
        assertThat(jdbc.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM posts WHERE body LIKE 'Test%'").query(Long.class).single()).isZero();
    }
}

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.status;

class FeedContractTest extends ApiTest {

    @Test
    void theFirstPageIsTheNewestPosts() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/feed")).andExpect(status().isOk())
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.posts", hasSize(20)))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.posts[0].id").value(100000)).andExpect(jsonPath("$.posts[0].author").value("asha_writes"))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.posts[0].body").value("Post number 100000")).andExpect(jsonPath("$.posts[0].createdAt").value("2026-10-01T05:33:20Z"))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.posts[19].id").value(99981)).andExpect(jsonPath("$.nextCursor").isString());
    }

    @Test
    void theCursorContinuesExactlyWhereThePageStopped() throws Exception {
        JsonNode first = getFeed(null, 7);
        JsonNode second = getFeed(first.get("nextCursor").asString(), 7);
        assertThat(first.get("posts").get(6).get("id").asLong()).isEqualTo(99994);
        assertThat(second.get("posts").get(0).get("id").asLong()).isEqualTo(99993);   // same second as 99994: the id breaks the tie
    }

    @Test
    void walkingTheLastThousandPostsShowsEachOnceAndEndsWithNoCursor() throws Exception {
        Set<Long> seen = new HashSet<>();
        String cursor = getFeed(null, 50).get("nextCursor").asString();
        for (int page = 0; page < 19; page++) {
            JsonNode next = getFeed(cursor, 50);
            next.get("posts").forEach(p -> seen.add(p.get("id").asLong()));
            cursor = next.get("nextCursor").asString();
        }
        assertThat(seen).hasSize(950);
        JsonNode nearEnd = json.readTree(mvc.perform(get("/feed").param("limit", "50").param("cursor", new Cursor(java.time.Instant.parse("2026-10-01T00:00:01Z"), 6).encode()))
                .andReturn().getResponse().getContentAsString());
        assertThat(nearEnd.get("posts")).hasSize(5);   // posts 1 to 5, the oldest

                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.posts", empty())).andExpect(jsonPath("$.nextCursor", nullValue()));

Shared setup, the EXPLAIN row counter and a feed helper.

package com.chaupal.feed;

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureMockMvc;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Import;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;
import tools.jackson.databind.JsonNode;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Shared setup: the whole app on a real PostgreSQL with the demo feed: 100,000 posts, five per second, so every
 * timestamp is shared by five posts. Tests that add posts remove them again.
 */
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@Import(PostgresTestConfig.class)
abstract class ApiTest {

    @Autowired
    MockMvc mvc;
    @Autowired
    JdbcClient jdbc;
    @Autowired
    TransactionTemplate transaction;

    final JsonMapper json = JsonMapper.builder().build();

    /** Rows every scan in the plan really produced, from EXPLAIN ANALYZE, without parallel workers. */
    long rowsRead(String sql, Map<String, Object> params) {
        return transaction.execute(status -> {
            jdbc.sql("SET LOCAL max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0").update();
            String plan = jdbc.sql("EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON) " + sql).params(params).query(String.class).single();
            return scanned(json.readTree(plan).get(0).get("Plan"));
        });
    }

    private static long scanned(JsonNode node) {
        long rows = node.get("Node Type").asString().contains("Scan") ? node.get("Actual Rows").asLong() * node.get("Actual Loops").asLong() : 0;
        if (node.has("Plans")) {
            for (JsonNode child : node.get("Plans")) {
                rows += scanned(child);
            }
        }
        return rows;
    }

    JsonNode getFeed(String cursor, int limit) throws Exception {
        var request = org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.get("/feed").param("limit", String.valueOf(limit));
        if (cursor != null) {
            request.param("cursor", cursor);
        }
        return json.readTree(mvc.perform(request).andReturn().getResponse().getContentAsString());
    }

    void post(String body) {
        jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO posts (author_id, body, created_at) VALUES (1, ?, TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-10-02 00:00:00+00')").param(body).update();
    }
}

package com.chaupal.feed;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.web.server.ResponseStatusException;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.OffsetDateTime;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;
import java.util.List;

@Service
class Feed {

    record Post(long id, String author, String body, Instant createdAt) {
    }

    record Page(List<Post> posts, String nextCursor, String topCursor) {
        Page(List<Post> posts, String nextCursor) {
            this(posts, nextCursor, posts.isEmpty() ? null : new Cursor(posts.getFirst().createdAt(), posts.getFirst().id()).encode());
        }
    }

    static final String FIRST = """
            SELECT p.id, a.handle AS author, p.body, p.created_at FROM posts p JOIN authors a ON a.id = p.author_id
            ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC LIMIT :n""";

    /** Seek: start right after the cursor's post, in the index's order. No OFFSET, so no rows are read and thrown away. */
    static final String AFTER = """
            SELECT p.id, a.handle AS author, p.body, p.created_at FROM posts p JOIN authors a ON a.id = p.author_id
            WHERE (p.created_at, p.id) < (:createdAt, :id)
            ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC LIMIT :n""";

    /** Challenge 2: the posts after the cursor in time, oldest first, so the limit keeps the ones right after it. */
    static final String NEWER = """
            SELECT p.id, a.handle AS author, p.body, p.created_at FROM posts p JOIN authors a ON a.id = p.author_id
            WHERE (p.created_at, p.id) > (:createdAt, :id)
            ORDER BY p.created_at, p.id LIMIT :n""";

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;

    Feed(JdbcClient jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    /** Challenge 1: the same seek, for one author. */
    Page page(Cursor after, int limit, String author) {
        if (author == null) {
            return page(after, limit);
        }
        Long authorId = jdbc.sql("SELECT id FROM authors WHERE handle = ?").param(author).query(Long.class).optional()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "No author " + author));
        String sql = (after == null ? FIRST : AFTER).replace("ORDER BY", (after == null ? "WHERE" : "AND") + " p.author_id = :author ORDER BY");
        var spec = jdbc.sql(sql).param("author", authorId).param("n", limit + 1);
        if (after != null) {
            spec = spec.param("createdAt", OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(after.createdAt(), ZoneOffset.UTC)).param("id", after.id());
        }
        return toPage(spec.query(Post.class).list(), limit);
    }

    /** Challenge 2. */
    Page newer(Cursor since, int limit) {
        List<Post> rows = new java.util.ArrayList<>(jdbc.sql(NEWER).param("createdAt", OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(since.createdAt(), ZoneOffset.UTC))
                .param("id", since.id()).param("n", limit).query(Post.class).list());
        java.util.Collections.reverse(rows);   // newest first, like the feed
        return rows.isEmpty() ? new Page(rows, null, new Cursor(since.createdAt(), since.id()).encode()) : new Page(rows, null);
    }

    Page page(Cursor after, int limit) {
        // One row more than asked: if it exists, there is a next page, and no count is needed.
        List<Post> rows = (after == null ? jdbc.sql(FIRST)
                : jdbc.sql(AFTER).param("createdAt", OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(after.createdAt(), ZoneOffset.UTC)).param("id", after.id()))
                .param("n", limit + 1).query(Post.class).list();
        return toPage(rows, limit);
    }

    private static Page toPage(List<Post> rows, int limit) {
        if (rows.size() <= limit) {
            return new Page(rows, null);
        }
        List<Post> page = rows.subList(0, limit);
        Post last = page.getLast();
        return new Page(page, new Cursor(last.createdAt(), last.id()).encode());
    }
}

import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.OffsetDateTime;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;
import java.util.List;

@Service
class Feed {

    record Post(long id, String author, String body, Instant createdAt) {
    }

    record Page(List<Post> posts, String nextCursor, String topCursor) {
        Page(List<Post> posts, String nextCursor) {
            this(posts, nextCursor, posts.isEmpty() ? null : new Cursor(posts.getFirst().createdAt(), posts.getFirst().id()).encode());
        }
    }

    static final String FIRST = """
            SELECT p.id, a.handle AS author, p.body, p.created_at FROM posts p JOIN authors a ON a.id = p.author_id
            ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC LIMIT :n""";

    /** Seek: start right after the cursor's post, in the index's order. No OFFSET, so no rows are read and thrown away. */

            WHERE (p.created_at, p.id) > (:createdAt, :id)
            ORDER BY p.created_at, p.id LIMIT :n""";

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;

    Feed(JdbcClient jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    /** Challenge 1: the same seek, for one author. */
    Page page(Cursor after, int limit, String author) {
        if (author == null) {
            return page(after, limit);
        }
        Long authorId = jdbc.sql("SELECT id FROM authors WHERE handle = ?").param(author).query(Long.class).optional()
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "No author " + author));
        String sql = (after == null ? FIRST : AFTER).replace("ORDER BY", (after == null ? "WHERE" : "AND") + " p.author_id = :author ORDER BY");
        var spec = jdbc.sql(sql).param("author", authorId).param("n", limit + 1);
        if (after != null) {
            spec = spec.param("createdAt", OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(after.createdAt(), ZoneOffset.UTC)).param("id", after.id());
        }
        return toPage(spec.query(Post.class).list(), limit);
    }

    /** Challenge 2. */
    Page newer(Cursor since, int limit) {
        List<Post> rows = new java.util.ArrayList<>(jdbc.sql(NEWER).param("createdAt", OffsetDateTime.ofInstant(since.createdAt(), ZoneOffset.UTC))
                .param("id", since.id()).param("n", limit).query(Post.class).list());
        java.util.Collections.reverse(rows);   // newest first, like the feed
        return rows.isEmpty() ? new Page(rows, null, new Cursor(since.createdAt(), since.id()).encode()) : new Page(rows, null);
    }

    Page page(Cursor after, int limit) {

    private static Page toPage(List<Post> rows, int limit) {
        if (rows.size() <= limit) {
            return new Page(rows, null);
        }
        List<Post> page = rows.subList(0, limit);
        Post last = page.getLast();
        return new Page(page, new Cursor(last.createdAt(), last.id()).encode());
    }
}

package com.chaupal.feed;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.Max;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Min;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Size;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
class FeedController {

    private final Feed feed;

    FeedController(Feed feed) {
        this.feed = feed;
    }

    /** Newest first. Pass the response's nextCursor to get the following page; null means the end. */
    @GetMapping("/feed")
    Feed.Page feed(@RequestParam(required = false) @Size(max = 100) String cursor,
                   @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") @Min(1) @Max(50) int limit,
                   @RequestParam(required = false) @Size(max = 30) String author) {
        return feed.page(cursor == null ? null : Cursor.decode(cursor), limit, author == null ? null : author.toLowerCase(java.util.Locale.ROOT));
    }

    /** Challenge 2: pull to refresh. */
    @GetMapping("/feed/new")
    Feed.Page newer(@RequestParam @Size(max = 100) String cursor, @RequestParam(defaultValue = "50") @Min(1) @Max(50) int limit) {
        return feed.newer(Cursor.decode(cursor), limit);
    }
}

Challenge 3 · design on paper, no code

Should the cursor be signed?

Anyone can decode the cursor and write their own. Here that only lets them start at any point in a public feed. When would it matter: a feed of private posts, a cursor that also carries filters or a user id, a cursor that expires? Compare an HMAC-signed cursor, an encrypted one, and a server-side cursor id stored for a few minutes.

  • 8. Implementation approach
  • 9. Design alternatives and trade-offs
  • 12. Database design: tables, constraints, indexes

The learner decides the design here, before opening the Code tab.

Implementation approach

  1. Write the trap test: the cost of a deep offset, repeats under new posts, and a time-only cursor.
  2. Pick the order (created_at, id) and an index for it.
  3. Seek with a row-value comparison; fetch one extra row.
  4. Encode the position in an opaque, versioned cursor, parsed strictly.

Design alternatives and trade-offs

ApproachWhat it costsVerdict
Keyset on (created_at, id), opaque cursorNo page numbers, no jumping.Chosen
OFFSETSlower each page; repeats and gaps under inserts.The trap
Cursor on time onlySkips posts sharing a timestamp.The trap, version 2
Cursor on id onlyCorrect only if ids follow time exactly, which imports and clock skew break.Fragile
Two conditions instead of a row value: created_at < t OR (created_at = t AND id < i)Same result; easier to get wrong; may plan worse.Works

Database design

ObjectWhatWhy
posts_feedB-tree (created_at, id)The feed order, read backwards; the seek starts inside it.
created_attimestamptz, default now()The database's clock, to the microsecond.
posts_author_fk, posts_body_not_blank, authors_handle_unique, authors_handle_shapeConstraintsNo orphan or empty posts.
CREATE TABLE authors (
    id     BIGINT      PRIMARY KEY,
    handle VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL CONSTRAINT authors_handle_unique UNIQUE
                               CONSTRAINT authors_handle_shape CHECK (handle ~ '^[a-z0-9_]{3,30}$')
);

CREATE TABLE posts (
    id         BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    author_id  BIGINT        NOT NULL CONSTRAINT posts_author_fk REFERENCES authors (id),
    body       VARCHAR(500)  NOT NULL CONSTRAINT posts_body_not_blank CHECK (btrim(body) <> ''),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ   NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- The feed's order, newest first: read backwards, (created_at, id) finds "the posts after this one" directly.
CREATE INDEX posts_feed ON posts (created_at, id);

A Working Systems station: the considerations to know, no runbook.

Deleted posts
A cursor still works if its post is deleted: it is a position, not a lookup.
Edits
Ordering by a column that changes ("updated at") moves posts between pages; order by something that never changes.
Clocks
With several app servers, use the database's now() (as here), not each server's clock.
Caching
The first page changes constantly; later pages by cursor barely do, and cache well.

  • 16. Interview takeaways
  • 17. Self-check rubric

Answers are hidden until opened, so the learner tries first.

Interview takeaways

Why does OFFSET get slower?

The database must produce and discard every skipped row in order; page N costs N × page size rows.

What is keyset pagination?

The next page is "rows after this key" in a fixed order, answered by an index seek; its cost does not grow with depth.

Why include the id in the cursor?

To break ties: several rows can share a timestamp, and the cursor must name exactly one position.

Why make the cursor opaque?

Clients cannot depend on its contents, so the server can change them; it also stops clients building offsets.

What does keyset pagination give up?

Jumping to page N and showing "page 3 of 100"; it suits feeds and exports, not numbered admin lists.
